title: Before I was formed (Berakhot 17a)
hookLine: Rava's Yom Kippur prayer: before I was formed I was nothing, and now I am as if unformed
tomorrow: the scholar or the farmer: who did more today?

cards: College essay advice, every fall: sell yourself. Name your wins. Take up space.
Now here's a sentence from the Talmud that walks the other way, and it's strange on purpose.

Rava, a sage with students and a name, ended his prayer like this: before I was formed, I was not worthy, and now that I have been formed, it's as if I had not been formed. So how can a grown man call himself unformed?

teach.b: Here's the rest of it, in plain words. Dust I am in my life, all the more so in my death. Here I am before You like a vessel full of shame.

May it be Your will that I not sin again, and what I have sinned, wipe away in Your mercy, but not through suffering. The Talmud adds that Rav Hamnuna Zuti said these same words on Yom Kippur. Now the puzzle.
One traditional reading solves it like this. Before I existed, nothing required me to exist.
Now that I'm here, I haven't yet become what I was made for, so it's as if I'm still unfinished. It isn't a sentence about being worthless. It's a sentence about being in progress.
Then the second strange line: dust I am in my life. Rava is alive, and he says dust anyway.
He's standing where Abraham stood, who told God he was "but dust and ashes," in Genesis: "who am but dust and ashes." Here's what's worth telling a friend tonight.
This humble prayer still asks for something big: wipe it away, and spare me the suffering. The humility doesn't shrink the request.
It's what makes the honest request possible. So the essay coach and Rava aren't really arguing. One is talking to an admissions office.

how: Rava's words, beginning Elohai ad shelo notzarti, are said in the Yom Kippur prayers in many prayer books, near the confession.

games.q: what does “before i was formed” mean?
o: a sage's humble prayer: unfinished in life, asking mercy
a mourner's prayer said beside a grave in Babylonia
a teaching about how the world was made out of nothing

games.q: Rava's prayer, line by line — tap the pairs.
p: as if I had not been formed
said the same words on Yom Kippur

s: Rava's prayer says people are worthless
in one traditional reading it says unfinished: formed, but not yet what he was made for.
'dust I am' in this prayer is only about death
Rava says dust in my life, and all the more so in my death.
the humble prayer still asks for something big
wipe away what I've sinned, in mercy, and not through suffering.

games.q: your friend wins an award, and at dinner says, "i'm nothing special, it was luck." is that what Rava's prayer is doing?
o: not quite: Rava speaks to God about being unfinished, and still asks for mercy.
yes: Rava teaches that you should brush off every good thing about yourself.
no: Rava's prayer is only about death, so it has nothing to say about awards.
games.why: Rava says dust in his life, before God, in a prayer that asks for something. it's honesty about being in progress, not a way to dodge a compliment.

practice: Say one humble sentence out loud, softly, that's true about you right now: where you're still unfinished, still learning. Rava said his to God; yours can go wherever it goes. Then let it stay in the room without fixing it.

wordCard.voice: Before I was formed. Rava's prayer after his prayer: not yet what he was made to be, dust in his life, and still asking for mercy.

orig.note: Hebrew: dust. Rava: dust I am in my life, all the more so in my death.

carryVoice: Pocket line: dust while alive, unfinished and still asking. Thirteen of fifty, and the tractate keeps going.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (Rava after his prayer: before I was formed I was not worthy…; Rav Hamnuna Zuti said it on Yom Kippur)
